Guessing a Column's Type

guess-data-type.Rmd

The chooser above the detectors

The Data-Type Detector Guide describes the detector library: dozens of pure predicates that each answer one yes/no question about a column (is_currency_code(), is_iso_date(), is_county_fips(), …). guess_data_type() sits above them. Given a column of values, it runs the whole library, ranks what matched, and returns a single best guess anchored to the ontology — the function create_dgf() leans on to make its first pass at typing a dataset.

g <- guess_data_type(c("USD", "EUR", "JPY", "GBP"))
g$guess
#> [1] "currency_code"
g$ontology
#>     data_type  data_subtype    data_class   data_format 
#> "categorical"     "nominal"    "category"        "code"

The guess is a detector name ("currency_code"); the ontology coordinates say what that means for governance — a currency code is a categorical code, not a number. The full return value carries the evidence behind the call:

str(g, max.level = 1)
#> List of 5
#>  $ guess     : chr "currency_code"
#>  $ ontology  : Named chr [1:4] "categorical" "nominal" "category" "code"
#>   ..- attr(*, "names")= chr [1:4] "data_type" "data_subtype" "data_class" "data_format"
#>  $ confidence: num 1
#>  $ candidates:'data.frame':  1 obs. of  5 variables:
#>  $ n         : int 4
  • guess — the winning detector, or NA when nothing is confident enough.
  • ontology — c(data_type, data_subtype, data_class, data_format) for the guess.
  • confidence — the winner’s pass rate (share of values it matched).
  • candidates — every type that cleared the reporting floor, ranked.
  • n — how many unique values were actually scored.

How it decides

Four steps, designed to stay cheap on a big dataset:

  1. Dedupe + sample. Only the unique non-missing values are scored, and at most n_sample of them (default 100). Scoring a million-row column costs the same as scoring its distinct values.
  2. Fast tier first. The fast detectors run first; the slow tier (fuzzy matchers) is consulted only if nothing fast clears threshold. (No detectors are slow today, so this is currently a single pass.)
  3. Rank with tie-breakers. Candidates are ordered by pass rate, then by a variable-name hint, then by specificity (a loose, catch-many detector loses a tie to a precise one).
  4. Map to the ontology. The winning detector name is resolved to its ontology coordinates.

The raw first step is exposed on its own as score_data_type(), which returns every detector’s pass rate against a set of values:

score_data_type(c("USD", "EUR", "XYZ"))[1, ]
#>       data_type n pass_rate
#> 1 currency_code 3 0.6666667

The name hint breaks ties the data can’t

Some values match more than one type. A five-digit code like 06037 is a valid ZIP and a valid county FIPS — both detectors pass at 100%. The data alone cannot choose; the variable name can:

vals <- c("06037", "36061", "48201", "17031")

guess_data_type(vals, name = "county_fips")$guess
#> [1] "county_fips"
guess_data_type(vals, name = "zip_code")$guess
#> [1] "zip_code"

Look at the ranked candidates to see why. Both types pass at 1.0, so the name_match column casts the deciding vote:

guess_data_type(vals, name = "county_fips")$candidates
#>     data_type n pass_rate name_match specific
#> 1 county_fips 4         1       TRUE    FALSE
#> 2    zip_code 4         1      FALSE     TRUE

With no name supplied, the tie falls to the more specific detector, so a bare column of five-digit codes is not silently mislabeled by whichever type happens to sort first.

Confidence, and the threshold / floor knobs

When nothing matches well, the honest answer is “I don’t know”:

guess_data_type(c("apple", "banana", "cherry"))$guess
#> [1] NA

Two thresholds control how bold the guess is:

  • threshold (default 0.8) — the top type must match at least this share of values to be reported as the guess; below it, guess is NA.
  • floor (default 0.5) — the minimum pass rate for a type to even appear in candidates.

Lower the threshold to accept a messier column; raise it to demand near-uniform matches. Because scoring is separated from the decision, you can also inspect candidates yourself and apply your own rule.

# a column that is 3/4 ISO dates: unknown at the default, a date if you relax it
messy <- c("2016-03-15", "2016-03-13", "1999-12-31", "not a date")
guess_data_type(messy)$guess               # NA (below 0.8)
#> [1] NA
guess_data_type(messy, threshold = 0.7)$guess
#> [1] "iso_date"

Where it is used

create_dgf() calls guess_data_type() once per column (via guess_dgf_types()), passing the variable name as the hint, to seed each variable’s desired_data_type / subtype / class and to flag near-unique keys. You then correct what the data alone could not reveal — see the Rule-Based Data Governance vignette for that workflow, and the Data-Type Detector Guide for the predicates underneath.
